slides.text:
A parameter is a named input of a function. The function declares it, and every call fills it with an **argument**.

The snippet is pseudo code, not Rust.

Rust is strict about parameters:

- every one has a name and a type
- arguments go by position, there are no names at the call
- there are no default values
- the count and the types must match

exercises.title: One parameter
exercises.guide: Give a function an input and call it with different values.

chunks.guide: A function that takes the floor number as input.

notes.text: A parameter is a name, a colon and its type.

chunks.guide: Call it twice. Each argument fills the parameter.

output.text:
Arriving at floor 3
Arriving at floor 12

exercises.title: Two parameters
exercises.guide: Take two inputs and compute from both.

chunks.guide: Parameters are separated by commas, and each one has its own type.

notes.text: Repeat the type even when two parameters share it.

chunks.guide: The arguments are matched to the parameters in order.

exercises.title: Complete the signature
exercises.guide: Give the second parameter its type, then divide the distance by it.

exercises.title: Order of arguments
exercises.explanation: Arguments fill the parameters by position: `high` is 3 and `low` is 10, so the result is 3 - 10.

exercises.title: Mixed types
exercises.guide: Parameters can all have different types.

chunks.guide: A sensor reading with an id, a temperature and an alarm flag.

notes.text: Each argument must match the type of its parameter.

chunks.guide: One argument of each type, in the same order as the signature.

exercises.title: A valid call
exercises.guide: Which call of `area` is accepted by Rust?
exercises.explanation: Two `f64` values by position. An integer literal is not a float, a call needs every argument, and Rust has no named arguments.

slides.text:
Inside the function, a parameter is an ordinary local variable, so the rules of variables apply: it is immutable unless declared `mut`.

With numbers, bools and chars the function receives a copy of the value.

A parameter can be shadowed like any variable, and its place in the signature can hold a pattern, so a tuple can be split into names right there.

The arguments themselves can be any expression of the right type.

exercises.title: Expressions as arguments
exercises.guide: Pass variables, constants and calculations as arguments.

chunks.guide: A price per kilogram, to pass to the function.
Shipping cost from the weight and the rate.
An argument can be any expression. It is computed before the call.

notes.text: Computed first, then handed to the parameter.

exercises.title: A mutable parameter
exercises.guide: Change a parameter inside the function and see what the caller keeps.

chunks.guide: A runner loses stamina every lap. The parameter is changed, so it is `mut`.

notes.text: Lets the function change its own copy.

chunks.guide: The function worked on a copy, so the original is untouched.

exercises.title: Change a parameter
exercises.guide: The function lowers its own copy of the tank. Fill in what allows it.

exercises.title: Shadow a parameter
exercises.guide: Redeclare parameters with a new type to compute with them.

chunks.guide: The parameters are integers, but an average needs floats. Shadow them with `f64` versions.

notes.text: A new sum, as a float, replaces the parameter.

exercises.title: Shadowed parameter
exercises.explanation: The parameter 5 is shadowed by 10. The inner block shadows it again with 11, and that ends with the block, so 10 is back.

exercises.title: Split a tuple argument
exercises.guide: Take a tuple as one argument and split it in the signature.

chunks.guide: One point in, two names out.

notes.text: A pattern in place of a name splits the tuple.

chunks.guide: Pass a tuple literal, then a tuple in a variable.
